words.gloss: branch of mathematics that uses letters for unknown numbers
words.ex: 1550s, from Medieval Latin algebra, from Arabic al jabr ("in vulgar pronunciation, al-jebr" ) "reunion of broken parts," as in computation, used 9c.

words.gloss: narrow, light boat paddled by hand
words.ex: 1550s, originally in a West Indian context, from Spanish canoa, a term used by Columbus, from Arawakan (Haiti) canaoua. Extended to rough-made or dugout boats generally.

words.gloss: basic unit of money in the US and several other countries
words.ex: 1550s, from Low German daler, from German taler (1530s, later thaler), abbreviation of Joachimstaler, literally "(gulden) of Joachimstal," coin minted 1519 from silver from mine opened 1516 near Joachimstal, town in Erzgebirge…

words.gloss: sleek vessel built for pleasure sailing or racing
words.ex: 1550s, yeaghe "a light, fast-sailing ship," from Norwegian jaght or early Dutch jaght, both from Middle Low German jacht, shortened form of jachtschip "fast pirate ship," literally "ship for chasing," from jacht "chase," from…

words.gloss: starchy tuber, baked, boiled or fried
words.ex: 1560s, from Spanish patata, from a Carib language of Haiti batata "sweet potato." Sweet potatoes were first to be introduced to Europe; in cultivation in Spain by mid-16c.; in Virginia by 1648. Early 16c.

words.gloss: large predatory sea fish with a fin on its back
words.ex: 1560s, of uncertain origin; apparently the word and the first specimen were brought to London by Capt. John Hawkins's second expedition (landed 1565; see Hakluyt).

words.gloss: four-stringed instrument played with a bow
words.ex: 1570s, from Italian violino, diminutive of viola (see viola). The modern form of the smaller, medieval viola da braccio.

words.gloss: explosive device
words.ex: 1580s, from French bombe, from Italian bomba, probably from Latin bombus "a deep, hollow noise; a buzzing or booming sound," from Greek bombos "deep and hollow sound," echoic. Originally of mortar shells, etc.…

words.gloss: public outrage caused by shocking wrongdoing
words.ex: 1580s, "discredit caused by irreligious conduct," from Middle French scandale (12c.), from Late Latin scandalum "cause for offense, stumbling block, temptation," from Greek skandalon "a trap or snare laid for an enemy," in New…

words.gloss: leaves dried for smoking or chewing
words.ex: 1580s, from Spanish tabaco, in part from an Arawakan language of the Caribbean (probably Taino), said to mean "a roll of tobacco leaves" (according to Las Casas, 1552) or "a kind of pipe for smoking tobacco"…

words.gloss: everything that exists: space, matter, energy
words.ex: 1580s, "the whole world, cosmos, the totality of existing things," from Old French univers (12c.), from Latin universum "all things, everybody, all people, the whole world," noun use of neuter of adjective universus "all…

words.gloss: giant woody grass with hollow stems
words.ex: 1590s, from Dutch bamboe, from Portuguese bambu, earlier mambu (16c.), probably from Malay samambu, though some suspect this is itself an imported word.

words.gloss: long curved yellow fruit
words.ex: 1590s, borrowed by Spanish or Portuguese from a West African word, possibly Wolof banana. The plant was introduced to the New World from Africa in 1516. Top banana, second banana, etc.

words.gloss: tax charged on imported goods
words.ex: 1590s, "arithmetical table," also "official list of customs duties on imports or exports…

words.gloss: platform sticking out from an upper wall of a building
words.ex: 1610s, from Italian balcone, from balco "scaffold," from a Germanic source (perhaps Langobardic *balko- "beam," cognate with Old English balca "beam, ridge;" see balk (n.)) + Italian augmentative suffix -one. Till c.

words.gloss: official count of a population
words.ex: 1610s, from Latin census "the enrollment of the names and property assessments of all Roman citizens," originally past participle of censere "to assess" (see censor (n.)).

words.gloss: large hard-shelled tropical fruit with milky juice
words.ex: 1610s, from coco + nut. Meaning "the head" is slang from 1834.

words.gloss: fertile spot with water in a desert
words.ex: 1610s, from French oasis (18c.) and directly from Late Latin oasis, from Greek oasis, probably from Hamitic (compare Coptic wahe, ouahe "oasis," properly "dwelling place," from ouih "dwell").

words.gloss: enclosed ground for sports or shows
words.ex: 1620s, "place of combat," from Latin harena "place of combat," originally "sand, sandy place," perhaps from Etruscan. The central stages of Roman amphitheaters were strewn with sand to soak up the blood.

words.gloss: place where outpatients get medical care
words.ex: 1620s, from French clinique (17c.), from Latin clinicus "physician that visits patients in their beds," from Greek klinike (techne) "(practice) at the sickbed," from klinikos "of the bed," from kline "bed, couch, that on which…

words.gloss: tower with a powerful beam that warns ships
words.ex: 1620s, from light (n.) + house (n.).

words.gloss: envelope of gases surrounding a planet
words.ex: 1630s, atmosphaera (modern form from 1670s), from Modern Latin atmosphaera, from atmo-, comb. form of Greek atmos "vapor, steam" + spharia "sphere" (see sphere).

words.gloss: set of rooms for living, part of a larger building
words.ex: 1640s, "private rooms for the use of one person within a house," from French appartement (16c.), from Italian appartimento, literally "a separated place," from appartere "to separate," from a "to" (see ad-) + parte "side, place,"…

words.gloss: facts and figures collected for analysis
words.ex: 1640s, plural of datum, from Latin datum "(thing) given," neuter past participle of dare "to give" (see date (n.1)). Meaning "transmittable and storable computer information" first recorded 1946. Data processing is from 1954.

words.gloss: instrument that makes distant objects look closer
words.ex: 1640s, from Italian telescopio (Galileo, 1611), and Modern Latin telescopium (Kepler, 1613), both from Greek teleskopos "far-seeing," from tele- "far" (see tele-) + -skopos "watcher" (see scope (n.1)).

words.gloss: fibrous mineral once used for fireproofing
words.ex: 1650s, earlier albeston, abestus (c. 1100), name of a fabulous stone, which, set afire, could not be extinguished…

words.gloss: goods carried by a ship, plane or truck
words.ex: 1650s, "freight loaded on a ship," from Spanish cargo "burden," from cargar "to load, impose taxes," from Late Latin carricare "to load on a cart" (see charge (v.)). South Pacific cargo cult is from 1949.

words.gloss: small breed of horse
words.ex: 1650s, powny, from Scottish, apparently from obsolete French poulenet "little foal" (mid-15c.), diminutive of Old French poulain "foal," from Late Latin pullanus "young of an animal," from Latin pullus "young of a horse, fowl,…

words.gloss: outline of what a course will cover
words.ex: 1650s, "table of contents of a series of lectures, etc.," from Late Latin syllabus "list," ultimately a misreading of Greek sittybos "parchment label, table of contents," of unknown origin. The misprint appeared in a 15c.

words.gloss: bluish-white metal used to galvanize steel
words.ex: 1650s, zinke, from German Zink, perhaps related to Zinke "prong, point;" said to have been used first by Paracelsus (c. 1526) on analogy of the form of its crystals after smelting.

words.gloss: classical dance of precise, graceful steps
words.ex: 1660s, from French ballette from Italian balletto, diminutive of ballo "a dance" (see ball (n.2)). Balletomane attested by 1930.

words.gloss: sparkling wine from northeastern France
words.ex: 1660s, from French, short for vin de Champagne "wine made in Champagne," former province in northwest France, literally "open country" (see campaign (n.)).

words.gloss: daily or weekly printed sheets of news
words.ex: 1660s, though the thing itself is older (see gazette); from news (n.) + paper (n.).

words.gloss: sweet flavoring from an orchid's seed pods
words.ex: 1660s, "pod of the vanilla plant," from Spanish vainilla "vanilla plant," literally "little pod," diminutive of vaina "sheath," from Latin vagina "sheath of an ear of grain, hull of a plant" (see vagina).

words.gloss: a thousand million
words.ex: 1680s, from French billion (originally byllion in Chuquet's unpublished "Le Triparty en la Science des Nombres," 1484; copied by De la Roche, 1520); see bi- "two" + million.

words.gloss: person forced to flee their country
words.ex: 1680s, from French refugié, noun use of past participle of refugier "to take shelter, protect," from Old French refuge (see refuge).

words.gloss: foamy waves breaking on the shore
words.ex: 1680s, probably from earlier suffe (1590s), of uncertain origin. Originally used in reference to the coast of India, hence perhaps of Indic origin. Or perhaps a phonetic respelling of sough, which meant "a rushing sound."

words.gloss: step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
words.ex: 1690s, from French algorithme, refashioned (under mistaken connection with Greek arithmos "number") from Old French algorisme "the Arabic numeral system" (13c.), from Medieval Latin algorismus, a mangled transliteration of Arabic…

words.gloss: sturdy cotton twill used for jeans
words.ex: 1690s, from French serge de Nîmes "serge from Nîmes," town in southern France. Application to "coarse cotton cloth" is first recorded 1850 in American English. Denims "pants made of denim" recorded from 1868.

words.gloss: person who reports the news
words.ex: 1690s, "one whose work is to write or edit public journals or newspapers," from French journaliste (see journal (n.) + -ist). Journalier also occasionally has been used. Meaning "one who keeps a journal" is from 1712.

words.gloss: curved piece of glass that bends light
words.ex: 1690s, "glass to regulate light rays," from Latin lens (genitive lentis) "a lentil," on analogy of the double-convex shape. See lentil. Anatomical use, of the eye part, from 1719. Lens-cap is by 1882.

words.gloss: quantity of motion: mass times velocity
words.ex: 1690s, scientific use in mechanics, "quantity of motion of a moving body," from Latin momentum "movement, moving power" (see moment). Figurative use dates from 1782.

words.gloss: performance by one person alone
words.ex: 1690s, "piece of music for one voice or instrument," from Italian solo, literally "alone," from Latin solus "alone" (see sole (adj.)).

words.gloss: gland in the neck that regulates metabolism
words.ex: 1690s (in reference to both the cartilage and the gland), from Greek thyreoiedes "shield-shaped" (in khondros thyreoiedes "shield-shaped cartilage," used by Galen to describe the "Adam's apple" in the throat), from thyreos…

words.gloss: serious bodily injury or deep emotional shock
words.ex: 1690s, "physical wound," medical Latin, from Greek trauma "a wound, a hurt; a defeat," from PIE *trau-, extended form of root *tere- (1) "to rub, turn," with derivatives referring to twisting, piercing, etc. (see throw (v.)).

words.gloss: legal state of being unable to pay one's debts
words.ex: 1700, from bankrupt, "probably on the analogy of insolvency, but with -t erroneously retained in spelling, instead of being merged in the suffix ...." . Figurative use from 1761.

words.gloss: detailed written analysis and judgment of a work
words.ex: 1702, restored French spelling of 17c. critick "art of criticism" (see critic), ultimately from Greek kritike tekhne "the critical art."

words.gloss: small sweet baked treat
words.ex: 1703, American English, from Dutch koekje "little cake," diminutive of koek "cake," from Middle Dutch koke (see cake (n.)). Slang application to persons attested since 1920.

words.gloss: long heroic tale from medieval Iceland
words.ex: 1709, an antiquarians' revival to describe the medieval prose narratives of Iceland and Norway, from Old Norse saga "saga, story," cognate with Old English sagu "a saying" (see saw (n.2)).

words.gloss: flat case for carrying papers or drawings
words.ex: 1722, porto folio; 1719 as port folio, from Italian portafoglio "a case for carrying loose papers," from porta, imperative of portare "to carry" (see port (n.1)) + foglio "sheet, leaf," from Latin folium (see folio).

words.gloss: inflammation of the liver
words.ex: 1727, from Greek hepatos, genitive of hepar "liver," from PIE root *yekwr- (source also of Sanskrit yakrt, Avestan yakar, Persian jigar, Latin jecur, Old Lithuanian jeknos "liver") + -itis "inflammation."

words.gloss: warrior of feudal Japan
words.ex: 1727, from Japanese samurai "warrior, knight," originally the military retainer of the daimio, variant of saburai, nominal form of sabura(h)u "to be in attendance, to serve."

words.gloss: paper, pens and other writing supplies
words.ex: 1727, from stationery wares (c. 1680) "articles sold by a stationer," from stationer "seller of books and paper" (q.v.) + -y (1).

words.gloss: stretch of land and its physical features
words.ex: 1727, "ground for training horses," from French terrain "piece of earth, ground, land," from Old French (12c.), from Vulgar Latin *terranum, from Latin terrenum "land, ground," noun use of neuter of terrenus "of earth, earthly,"…

words.gloss: roll of tobacco leaves for smoking
words.ex: 1730, from Spanish cigarro (source also of French cigare), probably from Maya sicar "to smoke rolled tobacco leaves," from si'c "tobacco;" or from or influenced by Spanish cigarra "grasshopper, cicada" (on resemblance of shape),…

words.gloss: covered passage lined with shops or arches
words.ex: 1731 (as arcado, from 1640s), from Italian arcata "arch of a bridge," from arco "arc," from Latin arcus (see arc).

words.gloss: fever spread by mosquito bites
words.ex: 1740, from Italian mal'aria, from mala aria, literally "bad air," from mala "bad" (fem. of malo, from Latin malus; see mal-) + aria "air" (see air (n.1)). Probably first used by Italian physician Francisco Torti (1658-1741).

words.gloss: small printed booklet advertising something
words.ex: 1748, "pamphlet; short written work stitched together," from French brochure "a stitched work," from brocher "to stitch" (sheets together), from Old French brochier "to prick, jab, pierce," from broche "pointed tool, awl"…

words.gloss: meal eaten outdoors
words.ex: 1748 (in Chesterfield's "Letters"), but rare before c. 1800 as an English institution; originally a fashionable pot-luck social affair, not necessarily out of doors…

words.gloss: rules of polite behavior
words.ex: 1750, from French étiquette "prescribed behavior," from Old French estiquette "label, ticket" (see ticket (n.)).

words.gloss: first public appearance
words.ex: 1751, from French début "first appearance," a figurative use from débuter "make the first stroke at billiards," also "to lead off at bowls" (a game akin to bowling), 16c., from but "mark, goal," from Old French but "end"…

words.gloss: juicy red fruit eaten as a vegetable
words.ex: 1753, earlier tomate (c. 1600), from Spanish tomate (mid-16c.) from Nahuatl (Aztecan) tomatl "a tomato," said to mean literally "the swelling fruit," from tomana "to swell." Spelling probably influenced by potato (1565).

words.gloss: track of steel rails for trains
words.ex: 1757, from rail (n.1) + road. Originally "road laid with rails for heavy wagons (in mining)." The process itself (but not the word) seems to have been in use by late 17c.

words.gloss: filling placed between slices of bread
words.ex: 1762, said to be a reference to John Montagu (1718-1792), Fourth Earl Sandwich, who was said to be an inveterate gambler who ate slices of cold meat between bread at the gaming table during marathon sessions rather than get up…

words.gloss: person traveling for pleasure
words.ex: 1772, "one who makes a journey for pleasure, stopping here and there" (originally especially a travel-writer), from tour (n.) + -ist. Tourist trap attested from 1939, in Graham Greene. Related: Touristic.

words.gloss: dense tropical forest
words.ex: 1776, "dense growth of trees and other tangled vegetation," such as that of the swampy regions at the base of the Himalayas in India, from Hindi jangal "desert, forest, wasteland, uncultivated ground," from Sanskrit jangala-s…

words.gloss: online image or character representing a user
words.ex: 1784, "descent of a Hindu deity," from Sanskrit avatarana "descent" (of a deity to the earth in incarnate form), from ava- "off, down" (from PIE *au- (2) "off, away") + base of tarati "(he) crosses over," from PIE root *tere- (2)…

words.gloss: child who has just learned to walk
words.ex: 1793, agent noun from toddle. Toddlekins is from 1839.

words.gloss: smallest unit of a chemical compound
words.ex: 1794, "extremely minute particle," from French molécule (1670s), from Modern Latin molecula, diminutive of Latin moles "mass, barrier" (see mole (3)). For ending see -cule. A vague meaning at first…

words.gloss: small place serving coffee and light meals
words.ex: 1802, from French café "coffee, coffeehouse," from Italian caffe "coffee" (see coffee). The beverage was introduced in Venice by 1615 and in France from 1650s by merchants and travelers who had been to Turkey and Egypt.

words.gloss: large keyboard instrument with hammered strings
words.ex: 1803, from French piano (18c.), Italian piano, shortened forms of pianoforte (q.v.). As an adverb, "softly," in musical directions (superlative pianissimo), attested from 1680s. Piano wire attested from 1831.

words.gloss: spiritual teacher or trusted adviser
words.ex: 1806, gooroo, from Hindi guru "teacher, priest," from Sanskrit guru-s "one to be honored, teacher," from guru- "venerable, worthy of honor," literally "heavy, weighty," from PIE root *gwere- (2) "heavy" (see grave (adj.)).

words.gloss: light scented water for the skin
words.ex: 1814, Cologne water, loan-translation of French eau de Cologne, literally "water from Cologne," from the city in Germany (German Köln, from Latin Colonia Agrippina) where it was made, first by Italian chemist Johann Maria Farina,…

words.gloss: science of living things
words.ex: 1819, from Greek bios "life" (see bio-) + -logy. Suggested 1802 by German naturalist Gottfried Reinhold Treviranus (1776-1837), and introduced as a scientific term that year in French by Lamarck.

words.gloss: set of keys for typing or playing music
words.ex: 1819, from key (n.1) in sense of "mechanism of a musical instrument" + board (n.1). Originally of pianos, organs, etc., extended to other machines 1846. The verb is first recorded 1926 (implied in keyboarding).

words.gloss: system of stretching, breathing and meditation
words.ex: 1820, from Hindi yoga, from Sanskrit yoga-s, literally "union, yoking" (with the Supreme Spirit), from PIE root *yeug- "to join" (see jugular). Related: Yogic.

words.gloss: place where meals are cooked and served to customers
words.ex: 1821, from French restaurant "a restaurant," originally "food that restores," noun use of present participle of restaurer "to restore or refresh," from Old French restorer (see restore).

words.gloss: in Hindu and Buddhist belief, the force of deeds shaping one's fate
words.ex: 1827, in Buddhism, the sum of a person's actions in one life, which determines his form in the next; from Sanskrit karma "action, work, deed…

words.gloss: expert who studies the natural world
words.ex: 1834, a hybrid coined from Latin scientia (see science) by the Rev. William Whewell (1794-1866), English polymath, by analogy with artist, in the same paragraph in which he coined physicist (q.v.).

words.gloss: thin roll of tobacco in paper
words.ex: 1835, American English, from French cigarette (by 1824), diminutive of cigare "cigar" (18c.), from Spanish cigarro (see cigar). Spanish form cigarito, cigarita also was popular in English mid-19c.

words.gloss: list of dishes offered
words.ex: 1837, from French menu de repas "list of what is served at a meal," from Middle French menu (adj.) "small, detailed" (11c.), from Latin minutus "small," literally "made smaller," past participle of minuere "to diminish," from…

words.gloss: picture made with a camera
words.ex: 1839, "picture obtained by photography," coined by Sir John Herschel from photo- + -graph "instrument for recording; something written." It won out over other suggestions, such as photogene and heliograph.

words.gloss: person who eats no meat
words.ex: 1839, irregular formation from vegetable (n.) + -arian, as in agrarian, etc. "The general use of the word appears to have been largely due to the formation of the Vegetarian Society in Ramsgate in 1847" .

words.gloss: microscopic single-celled organisms
words.ex: 1847, plural of Modern Latin bacterium, from Greek bakterion "small staff," diminutive of baktron "stick, rod," from PIE *bak- "staff used for support" (also source of Latin baculum "rod, walking stick").

words.gloss: aircraft lifted by overhead spinning blades
words.ex: 1861, from French hélicoptère "device for enabling airplanes to rise perpendicularly," thus "flying machine propelled by screws." From Greek helix (genitive helikos) "spiral" (see helix) + pteron "wing" (see ptero-).

words.gloss: two-wheeled vehicle moved by pedals
words.ex: 1868, coined from bi- "two" + Greek kyklos "circle, wheel" (see cycle (n.)), on the pattern of tricycle; both the word and the vehicle superseding earlier velocipede.

words.gloss: reanimated corpse of folklore and horror
words.ex: 1871, of West African origin (compare Kikongo zumbi "fetish;" Kimbundu nzambi "god"), originally the name of a snake god, later with meaning "reanimated corpse" in voodoo cult.

words.gloss: study of how organisms relate to their surroundings
words.ex: 1873, oecology, "branch of science dealing with the relationship of living things to their environments," coined in German by German zoologist Ernst Haeckel (1834-1919) as Ökologie, from Greek oikos "house, dwelling place,…

words.gloss: addictive stimulant drug made from a South American shrub
words.ex: 1874, from Modern Latin cocaine (1856), coined by Albert Niemann of Gottingen University from coca (from Quechua cuca) + chemical suffix -ine (2).

words.gloss: Italian dough shaped into noodles, shells and tubes
words.ex: 1874, from Italian pasta, from Late Latin pasta "dough, pastry cake, paste," from Greek pasta "barley porridge," probably originally "a salted mess of food," from neuter plural of pastos (adj.) "sprinkled, salted," from passein…

words.gloss: informal word for a two-wheeler
words.ex: 1882, American English, shortened and altered form of bicycle.

words.gloss: slang for a guy or buddy
words.ex: 1883, "fastidious man," New York City slang of unknown origin; recent research suggests it is a shortening of Yankee Doodle, based on the song's notion of "foppish, over-fastidious male" (compare macaroni).

words.gloss: short written note in an office
words.ex: 1889, shortening of memorandum (q.v.).

words.gloss: world's most popular ball game, played with the feet
words.ex: 1889, socca, later socker (1891), soccer (1895), originally university slang (with jocular formation -er (3)), from a shortened form of Assoc., abbreviation of association in Football Association (as opposed to Rugby football)…

words.gloss: game of shooting a ball through a high hoop
words.ex: 1892, American English, from basket + ball (n.1). The game was invented 1891 by James A. Naismith (1861-1939), physical education instructor in Springfield, Massachusetts, U.S.

words.gloss: of engines that burn oil ignited by compression
words.ex: 1894, named for Rudolf Diesel (1858-1913), German mechanical engineer who designed this type of engine.

words.gloss: long-distance run of about 26 miles
words.ex: 1896, marathon race, from story of Greek hero Pheidippides, who in 490 B.C.E. ran the 26 miles and 385 yards to Athens from the Plains of Marathon to tell of the allied Greek victory there over Persian army.

words.gloss: huge sea wave caused by an undersea quake
words.ex: 1896, in reference to the one that struck Japan that year on June 15, from Japanese tsunami, from tsu "harbor" + nami "waves."

words.gloss: inert gas that glows red-orange in tubes
words.ex: 1898, coined by its discoverers, Sir William Ramsay and Morris W. Travers, from Greek neon, neuter of neos "new" (see new); so called because it was newly discovered. Neon sign is attested from 1927.

words.gloss: theater where films are shown
words.ex: 1899, "a movie hall," from French cinéma, shortened from cinématographe "motion picture projector and camera," coined 1890s by Lumiere brothers, who invented it, from Latinized form of Greek kinemat-, comb.

words.gloss: powered flying machine with fixed wings
words.ex: 1907, from air (n.1) + plane (n.1); though the original references are British, the word caught on in American English, where it largely superseded earlier aeroplane (1873 in this sense and still common in British English).

words.gloss: car with a driver hired for a fare
words.ex: 1907, shortening of taximeter cab (introduced in London in March 1907), from taximeter "automatic meter to record the distance and fare" (1898), from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (1890), coined from Medieval Latin taxa…

words.gloss: device that shows moving pictures broadcast from afar
words.ex: 1907, as a theoretical system to transmit moving images over telegraph or telephone wires; formed in English or borrowed from French télévision, from tele- + vision.

words.gloss: unit of heredity carried in DNA
words.ex: 1911, from German Gen, coined 1905 by Danish scientist Wilhelm Ludvig Johannsen (1857-1927), from Greek genea "generation, race," from PIE root *gene- (see genus). De Vries had earlier called them pangenes.

words.gloss: developmental condition affecting social communication
words.ex: 1912, from German Autismus, coined 1912 by Swiss psychiatrist Paul Bleuler (1857-1939) from comb. form of Greek autos- "self" (see auto-) + -ismos suffix of action or of state. The notion is of "morbid self-absorption."

words.gloss: film shown in a theater, in everyday American speech
words.ex: 1912 (perhaps 1908), shortened form of moving picture in the cinematographic sense (1896). As an adjective from 1913. Movie star attested from 1913. Another early name for it was photoplay.

words.gloss: bag carried on both shoulders
words.ex: 1914 as a noun, 1916 as a verb, from back (n.) + pack (n.). Related: Backpacked; backpacking.

words.gloss: nutrient needed in tiny amounts for health
words.ex: 1920, originally vitamine (1912) coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk (1884-1967), from Latin vita "life" (see vital) + amine, because they were thought to contain amino acids.

words.gloss: hormone that regulates blood sugar
words.ex: 1922 (earlier insuline, 1914), coined in English from Latin insula "island" (see isle and compare insula); so called because the hormone is secreted by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.

words.gloss: machine that performs tasks automatically
words.ex: 1923, from English translation of 1920 play "R.U.R." ("Rossum's Universal Robots"), by Karel Capek (1890-1938), from Czech robotnik "slave," from robota "forced labor, compulsory service, drudgery," from robotiti "to work,…

words.gloss: word puzzle with intersecting clues
words.ex: 1925, short for crossword puzzle (q.v.).

words.gloss: roadside lodging for motorists
words.ex: 1925, coined from motor- + hotel. Originally a hotel for automobile travelers.

words.gloss: capacity of a channel to carry data
words.ex: 1930, in electronics, from band (n.1) + width.

words.gloss: baked Italian flatbread with cheese and toppings
words.ex: 1935, from Italian pizza, originally "cake, tart, pie," of uncertain origin. The 1907 "Vocabolario Etimologico della Lingua Italiana" reports it is said to be from dialectal pinza "clamp" (from Latin pinsere "to pound, stamp").

words.gloss: strong synthetic fiber
words.ex: 1938, coined, according to DuPont, from random generic syllable nyl- + -on, common ending in fiber names (compare rayon), said to be ultimately from cotton. Use (in plural) for "nylon stockings" is from 1940.

words.gloss: field of designing and building automated machines
words.ex: 1941, from robot + -ics. Coined in a science fiction context by Russian-born U.S. author Isaac Asimov (1920-1992), who proposed the "Three Laws of Robotics" in 1968.

words.gloss: find and fix errors in code
words.ex: 1945, of machine systems, from de- + bug (n.) "glitch, defect in a machine." Meaning "to remove a concealed microphone" is from 1964. Related: Debugged; debugging.

words.gloss: use of machines to do work without human effort
words.ex: 1948, in the manufacturing sense, coined by Ford Motor Co. Vice President Delmar S. Harder, from automatic + -ion. Earlier (1838) was automatism, which meant "quality of being automatic" in the classical sense.

words.gloss: breathing gear for diving underwater
words.ex: 1952, acronym for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

words.gloss: eight bits of computer memory
words.ex: 1956, American English; see bit (n.2). Reputedly coined by Dr. Werner Buchholz at IBM.

words.gloss: intense, narrow beam of light
words.ex: 1960, acronym for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation," on pattern of maser (1955). A corresponding verb, lase, was coined by 1962. Related: Lasered; lasering. Laser disc recorded from 1980.

words.gloss: nightclub for dancing; also its pulsing music
words.ex: 1964, American English shortening of discotheque; sense extended by 1972 to the kind of music played there.

words.gloss: smallest dot of a screen image
words.ex: 1969, coined to describe the photographic elements of a television image, from pix + first syllable of element.

words.gloss: copy a file from a remote computer to your own
words.ex: 1977 (n.), 1980 (v.), from down (adv.) + load (v.). Related: Downloaded; downloading.

words.gloss: singing along to recorded backing music
words.ex: 1979, Japanese, from kara "empty" + oke "orchestra," the latter a shortened form of okesutora, which is a Japanning of English orchestra.

words.gloss: wired networking standard for computers
words.ex: 1980, from ether + ending as in Internet, etc.

words.gloss: handheld device that records video
words.ex: 1982, from camera and recorder.

words.gloss: person who manages a website
words.ex: 1993, from web in the Internet sense + master (n.).

words.gloss: online journal of regular posts
words.ex: 1998, short for weblog (which is attested from 1994, though not in the sense "online journal"), from (World Wide) Web + log. Joe Bloggs (c. 1969) was British slang for "any hypothetical person" (compare U.S. equivalent Joe Blow)…

words.gloss: downloadable audio show in episodes
words.ex: 2004, noun and verb, from pod-, from iPod, brand of portable media player, + second element abstracted from broadcast. Related: Podcasting.
